title: Is Python what makes this slow, and would Rust or Go help?

compiler_flags.rust: cargo build --release; [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort" (k3-k5's k5 crate omits panic=abort; k3 crate additionally enables the sha2/sha1 'asm' feature)
compiler_flags.go: plain `go build`, no non-default flags anywhere (GOFLAGS=-mod=mod and a local GOPATH only, to keep the module cache inside tmp/)
compiler_flags.fxhash: hand-rolled (rustc-hash algorithm) with a splitmix-style finalizer; the naive finalizer is a measured 600x footgun on packed symbol keys

answer.short: Yes for one stage, and a Rust port is worth a measured 20.1x against the shipped Python (band 20-27x) but only 5.2-7.0x against the best keep-the-Python stack, which is measured at 3.87x for ~50 lines plus a build step. Do the Python levers first. The rewrite decision is set by how far the alphabet migration is going, not by seconds per day.
answer.is_python_the_bottleneck: Yes, but only for the M1 settlement fixpoint. It is CPython to within the 0.61% unattributed-sample floor, strictly single-threaded, 337.9 s cold / 194.9 s warm, and ~60% of modelled foreground wait. make test (70.55% HarfBuzz, ceiling 1.23-1.40x) and make all (62.6% fontTools, ceiling 1.30x) are the opposite and must not be rewritten.
answer.would_rust_help: Yes, measurably: 20.07x single-threaded on a structurally faithful model, independently reproduced at 19.9x, with exact checksum AND call-counter equivalence in three languages. The fidelity discount (model Python is 0.754x the real kernel per kernel operation) makes 20x a floor; band 20-27x. Go is 16.1x and decays with volume, so its real-kernel figure is an upper bound.
answer.by_how_much_that_matters: Against the shipped Python: 20.1x serial, 43-71x with six-way configuration parallelism (derived; the 96.5x model figure is refuted). Against a levered Python (2.28x measured): 8.8x. Against levers+mypyc (3.87x measured): 5.2-7.0x, worth ~426-499 machine-seconds/day incremental on a ~2,040 s/day stage.
answer.recommendation_one_line: Do the Python levers now (gc + six memoizations + NamedTuple = 2.28x measured, byte-identical artifact, ~50 lines); re-baseline; then decide the port on the alphabet target, not on seconds per day.

multipliers.variant: python tuple of str|None + 4 frozen dataclasses / rust 10-byte packed struct + hand-rolled Fx map / go packed struct + built-in map

multipliers.kernel: K1 primitive: construct a 5-field settle.Candidate
multipliers.variant: python frozen dataclass / rust struct / go struct
multipliers.equivalence: Content checksum over 200,000 records identical in all three (5212379886543265401), computed in a separate untimed verify pass.

multipliers.kernel: K1 primitive: map insert on a 10-slot STRING key
multipliers.variant: python dict / rust HashMap / go map
multipliers.equivalence: 1,875,829 distinct entries in all three, from the real memo-key store.
multipliers.caveat: PYTHON WINS — CPython caches string hashes. The same insert on a packed u64 key is 4.82 ns in Rust (22.1x, and 32x faster than Python's best row). THE PACKING, NOT THE LANGUAGE, IS THE WIN. Python's row grows a dict from empty while the ports are presized, so the asymmetry runs against the ports, not for them.

multipliers.kernel: K1 primitive: map insert on a packed u64 key
multipliers.variant: python dict / rust HashMap / go map
multipliers.equivalence: Packed-key map proved lossless by a matching value-sum checksum.
multipliers.caveat: A hand-rolled FxHash with a bare finish() measured 25,744 ns/op — a 600x blowup vs SipHash — because this key's low bits are a 5-value alphabet. A splitmix-style finalizer brings it to 4.9-12.7 ns. A port must check this.

options_ranked.option: gc.freeze() + gc.disable() at run_m1's entry point
options_ranked.risk: Low. Peak RSS +15% (3.77 -> 4.34 GB) and nothing reclaims cycles for the run's duration; a longer-lived process would need a periodic manual gc.collect() or a freeze-then-leave-enabled variant, which was not measured.
options_ranked.verdict: DO IT. 1.14x measured twice at full scale on the real kernel, byte-identical digest, 15,692 collections that collect 12 objects in total.

options_ranked.option: Six memoizations + RightToken NamedTuple in settle.py (with #1: the lever stack)
options_ranked.risk: Medium-low. Introduces a returned-list aliasing invariant on candidates(); two scratch-patch blemishes must be fixed before landing (_PAIRING_SETS at module level with no cap — the repo's own _GUARD_STATES pattern caps at 8; P8 declares two caches it never uses). The full 1,162-test rebuild suite was not run, only the 182 kernel tests.
options_ranked.reversibility: Reversible — ~50 lines, one file pair, no new runtime and no new tool
options_ranked.verdict: DO IT. BEST RATIO OVERALL. Byte-identical artifact at full scale; 182/182 repo kernel tests pass including test_trace_memo, which drives build_tables through a real persisted TraceStore AND a live TraceShare. P6 (memoize candidates() on the collapsed left key) is the big one — 95.2% of its calls are redundant on that key. Two negative results already known: memoizing _prefer_favors is 0.79x, memoizing right2 option lists is inside the noise.

options_ranked.option: mypyc on model/specificity/settle/table, on top of #2
options_ranked.risk: Medium. mypy becomes a second type checker alongside pyright and the two disagree (pyright is green on code mypy rejects); a C toolchain and per-platform, per-CPython-version wheels become build inputs; inspect.getsource fails on every compiled function so pdb stepping into the kernel is gone; mypyc rejects class PartitionError(RuntimeError) outright, so mypy_extensions lands in table.py's runtime import path.
options_ranked.verdict: PROBABLY. The single largest keep-the-Python win and the last thing available before a port — but the first option with real ongoing cost. Seven source edits needed (five annotation widenings, one Literal cast, one escape hatch); build is cheap (7.8 s cold); 258 rebuild tests pass.

options_ranked.option: max_chars_after 2 -> 1 in the 17 sharded calt sweeps (tiered)
options_ranked.risk: COVERAGE, NOT PERFORMANCE. The blunt cut gives up 22 of 215 reachable pair renderings (18 of the 22 in three pairs); the tier keeping the eight depth-2-dependent tests gives up nothing TODAY, but nothing guards that it stays true as runes change. Whether any of the 22 could flip an actual assertion needs fault injection, which was not done.
options_ranked.verdict: PUT IT TO THE USER. Beats a full make test rewrite (ceiling 1.23-1.40x) by 2-3x, and no rewrite can reach it. depth2_states.py (47.9 s, one core) is offered as the guard but is not wired into any gate.

options_ranked.option: Cut-the-work bundle: os._exit after the M1 build's last write; lru_cache on build.config_badge; persist load_human_unit_ids in manifest.json; yaml.CSafeLoader at the hot call sites; signature_digest repr -> marshal
options_ranked.risk: Low, except signature_digest, which changes the digest bytes and re-stamps the persisted signature store once (partition verified identical over 400 real signatures).
options_ranked.verdict: DO THEM. Tiny prizes individually, excellent ratio, all verified output-identical. config_badge is 281x on 62,148 calls with 12 distinct argument tuples; load_human_unit_ids re-parses 264.5 MB to produce 10,622 ids; teardown after six configs is a measured 9.5 s.

options_ranked.risk: Coverage-neutral: the gate passes with 0 divergences and exact rule/transition coverage at h3, h4 and h5 alike.
options_ranked.verdict: HOLD. Two runs disagree on both magnitude and ordering. Becomes decisive at full migration — the sweep is Theta(A^H), so at A=47 horizon 5 is 234 M sequences per config against 5.0 M at horizon 4, and no rewrite substitutes for that.

options_ranked.risk: None today. The risk is entirely in the future: at letters^4.0-4.5 the six-config cold build reaches 6.9-11.9 hours at full migration.
options_ranked.verdict: The honest floor — and it beats rows 8, 9, 11 and 12 on ratio.

options_ranked.option: Free-threaded CPython 3.14t config-parallelism on top of #2
options_ranked.risk: High. uharfbuzz CANNOT be installed on 3.14t (no cp314t wheel; Py_LIMITED_API is incompatible with Py_GIL_DISABLED), and fontTools.feaLib.lexer re-enables the GIL process-wide on import — so it needs a narrower subprocess entry point or PYTHON_GIL=0. Six concurrent production fixpoints are ~20-23 GB (fits this 51.5 GB box, not a 16 GB one). It gives up the 1.9x cross-config share. The cap-8 _GUARD_STATES/_LIVENESS_PROBES LRUs evict each other's live entries under true concurrency.
options_ranked.verdict: NO — STRICTLY DOMINATED by row 3, which reaches the same 3.08x on ONE core instead of ~2.8. Thread-safety was audited and config-parallel threading is safe (every hot mutable object is per-Engine); sharing a single Engine across threads would silently corrupt the fired-provenance capture, which is the blocker for parallelising INSIDE a configuration.

options_ranked.option: Partial Rust port: K3 placed-ink layer only
options_ranked.risk: Low. Cleanest interface in the repo and checksum-verifiable against a declared byte-identity contract. One unreachable divergence: Python raises TypeError comparing None to a tuple inside a sort where Rust's Option<T> orders None first — unreachable on this corpus, but a font with TrueType qCurveTo off-curve points would exercise it.
options_ranked.verdict: NOT YET. A real 16.67x on the arithmetic, but 7.78x whole-kernel after the 7.3% HarfBuzz floor, on a ~65 s/day line. The pure-Python marshal lever takes a third of it for one line.

options_ranked.option: Full Rust port of the M1 settlement kernel (cut line at build_tables, file boundary, no FFI)
options_ranked.engineer_days: 30-60 (centred ~40) fluent; 60-100 learning; PLUS 6-12 engineer-days/month recurring duplication tax
options_ranked.risk: High, and the risk is NOT correctness — the verification story is unusually strong. The risk is a permanent second implementation of the product's core semantics: the port does not retire settle.py (19 non-test modules reference it; conform.py alone has 75 references and settles every swept text in Python; emit_gsub.py calls formation_blocked to generate shipped FEA rows), and the kernel is not finished (23 semantics commits in 2 months, flat to rising, at 350-500 lines each). 78.7% of runtime lives in one 336-line class whose wrong verdict omits windows silently. explain.py and probe.py would explain what Python thinks rather than what the font was built from. uv sync stops being sufficient to reproduce the project; CI never runs the rebuild pipeline, so the binary would be macOS-ARM-only in practice.
options_ranked.reversibility: The Python stays, so the binary is deletable — but the file format, toolchain and CI story are not
options_ranked.verdict: CONDITIONAL. Lowest ratio on today's workload; the only measured option that reaches a full alphabet. Decide it on the alphabet target, not on seconds per day. If it happens: Rust, not Go, with an arena for the memo and packed symbol-id keys.

options_ranked.risk: A second runtime for one subprocess; needs a NEW narrower entry point because run_m1 pulls fontTools and uharfbuzz; the repo's nine PEP 758 unparenthesized `except A, B:` clauses must be rewritten and requires-python relaxed from >=3.14 (there is no PyPy 3.14); peak RSS 5.39 GB vs CPython's 4.05 on one config.
options_ranked.verdict: DROP — not ranked. Actively worse than stock CPython once the memoizations land (1.74x vs 2.13x). Its one genuine credit: it eliminates the interpreter-teardown cost, 0.79 s against CPython's 2.62 s on one configuration.

options_ranked.risk: Everything the binary costs plus a compiled build in the dependency chain.
options_ranked.verdict: STRUCK, NOT WEIGHED — strictly dominated. Its only advantage over a subprocess is saving a serialization measured at ~2.5% of the build, and handing Python objects across the boundary rebuilds the exact 254.2 B -> 10 B object graph the packing exists to delete.

recommendation.headline: Do the Python levers now. Put the alphabet question to the user. Do not start a Rust port until that question is answered.

first_three_actions.action: gc.freeze() + gc.disable() at run_m1's entry point
first_three_actions.measured_worth: 1.14x on the real kernel at full 18-rune scale (81.25 -> 71.24 CPU-s, and independently 80.65 -> 70.45 in an interleaved fresh-process A/B), artifact digest byte-identical in all four arms
first_three_actions.note: Also settles cost-model adjudication #5: the GC share was real but the A/B offered as proof ran backwards in one rep under contention. Costs +15% peak RSS.

first_three_actions.action: The six memoizations plus the RightToken NamedTuple in settle.py
first_three_actions.measured_worth: 2.28x combined with action 1, on the real kernel at full scale (78.93 -> 34.66 CPU-s), digest 3026eaf52b6b87d6... identical in every arm, 182/182 repo kernel tests passing including test_trace_memo
first_three_actions.cost: ~50 lines, one file pair, no new runtime or tool, 3-8 engineer-days

first_three_actions.action: Re-baseline: one make artifact-cycle with cycle-timings.ndjson landing, after 1 and 2, plus one alphabet-scaling sweep
first_three_actions.measured_worth: Not seconds — honesty. It changes the Rust port's advantage from 20.1x to 5.2-8.8x, i.e. the difference between a decision made against 78.9 CPU-s and one made against 34.7 (or 20.4 with mypyc). It also closes the two largest holes in the cost model: gate:conform's real cost and the real build cadence, which this box's green records suggest may be far below the assumed one cycle per arming commit.
first_three_actions.note: Every rewrite number in this report is a ratio against a baseline that actions 1 and 2 move by 2.28x. No port should ever be benchmarked against the shipped denominator once the levered one exists.

recommendation.then: mypyc (option 3) is the next-best ratio and the last thing available before a port. The max_chars_after tier (option 4) is worth more foreground seconds than a full make test rewrite could ever buy and should be raised as the coverage decision it is.

duplication_tax.why_the_port_does_not_retire_settle_py: 19 non-test modules reference settle. conform.py has 75 references and constructs Engine + runs settle_with_engine per swept text; emit_gsub.py calls formation_blocked to generate the shipped formation-guard `ignore sub` rows; explain.py, probe.py, tablediff.py, unit_cache.py, drafts.py, enrich.py and manual_pins.py all drive the Python Engine.
duplication_tax.credit: three of the last five kernel commits (the fifty-minutes-to-twelve cut, the persisted trace memo, the cross-config share) exist ONLY because Python is slow and would never have been written at 20x; the next lever WHATNEXT names (persisting the liveness verdicts) would also become unnecessary. author_facing_costs: explain.py — the section 6.3a CLI whose entire value is replaying THE SAME code that built the table — would explain what Python thinks, not what the font was built from. Same for rebuild/tools/probe.py. Its TransitionTrace already carries ranked/eliminations/decided_stage/runner_up, so only the printing is Python.
settle.py's _incomparable_message (38 lines) prints a paste-ready YAML resolve stub when two prefer records conflict; that authoring UX lives inside the kernel.

uv sync stops being sufficient to reproduce the project. CI (.github/workflows/deploy.yml, ubuntu-latest) runs only pyright and tools/build_font.py and never touches the rebuild pipeline, so nothing breaks today — but the binary has no CI-built artifact and the M1 stage becomes macOS-ARM-only in practice.

language_choice.why: Rust's multiplier is flat across volume (19.8-20.7x) while Go's decays (18.3 -> 15.0x) as its GC scans a bigger live heap; the real kernel is 1.6x larger again and heading for 74-127x larger still. A memoized fixpoint whose entire working set stays live until the build ends is the worst possible shape for a tracing GC and the best possible shape for an arena. Peak RSS confirms it: 7.46 GB of live graph for six configs today.
